title: Lager styles
lead: Clean, crisp and cold: from pilsner to dark lager.

sections.name: Pilsner
know: Czech pilsner: rich malt, smooth bitterness.
German pils: drier, crisper, floral hops.

sections.name: American lager and light lager

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Pale, fizzy, light and served very cold.

know: Corn or rice keeps it light.

sections.name: Helles, Märzen and Oktoberfest

lines.label: In short
lines.text: German malty lagers, gold to amber.

know: Märzen: amber and toasty, the classic US “Oktoberfest”.
Festbier: the paler beer poured at Munich’s Oktoberfest today.

sections.name: Bock and dark lagers

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Strong bocks, and black beers that drink light.

know: Bock: strong and malty, about 6–7.5% ABV.
Schwarzbier: black but light, smooth roast.

read.where: Pilsner was first brewed in **Plzeň** (Pilsen), in today’s Czech Republic, in **1842**: the beer now sold as Pilsner Urquell. **Czech** pilsner is gold with rich malt and a strong but **smooth** bitterness from Czech hops (about 4.2–5.8% ABV). Germany’s **pils** came a few decades later: paler, **drier** and **crisper**, with a floral, spicy hop aroma.
read.mixup: Most mass-market “pilsner” lagers are closer to American lager: lighter and much less bitter.
read.sayIt: It’s a crisp pilsner: clean, a little bitter, really refreshing.

keyPoints.line: served colder than any other style.

read.bigIdea: Built to be light and cold.
read.where: **American light lager** is very pale, highly carbonated and very light in body, with very little bitterness: about **2.8–4.2% ABV**. Miller popularized it from **1973**. **American lager** is the same idea, slightly fuller, about **4.2–5.3%**. Both can use **corn or rice**. Serve them the **coldest** of any beer.
read.mixup: Light lager isn’t “watered down”. It’s brewed light on purpose.

read.bigIdea: German lagers that lead with malt.
read.where: **Munich Helles** (1894) is gold, smooth and **bready**, with gentle bitterness. **Märzen** is **amber** and **toasty**, with a dry finish: originally brewed in March and aged cold over summer. It’s the classic amber **Oktoberfest**, and still what most US breweries call Oktoberfest. Since 1990, most beer at Munich’s own Oktoberfest is **Festbier**: paler, gold and smooth.
read.mixup: Märzen and Oktoberfest are often the same beer in the US. In Munich today, the festival beer is paler.

read.bigIdea: Dark lagers are smooth, not heavy.
read.where: **Bock** is a **strong, malty** German lager, from the town of **Einbeck**: dark **Dunkles Bock** is toasty (about 6.3–7.2% ABV), pale **Maibock** a little hoppier. **Munich Dunkel** is **brown** and tastes of **bread crust**, with no burnt notes. **Schwarzbier** (“black beer”) is nearly black with smooth roast, but light and dry: it drinks **lighter than it looks**.
read.mixup: A black lager isn’t a stout. It’s lighter, crisper and less roasty.
read.sayIt: It looks like a stout, but it drinks light and smooth.

sources: BJCP 2021 Style Guidelines, 1A, 1B, 3B, 4A, 4B, 4C, 5D, 6A, 6C, 8A, 8B (bjcp.org); Cicerone, US Certified Beer Server Syllabus v6.0, 2024 (cicerone.org). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
